reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the creator presents a tutorial for a crypto bot that claims rapid, unusually high profits and instructs viewers to fund a smart contract through MetaMask. The video tells viewers to follow specific steps, including pasting an external contract into Remix, funding the created contract, and pressing an Action button to activate automated trading. It also claims results such as 9.4 BNB, 90 percent profit transfers, a 15x return, and potentially a thousand BNB per day, without verified contract behavior or returns.

citations.quote: I'll show you how I earned 9.4 BNB, that's almost 5.000 U$D, with a front running bot I created by myself.
PLEASE FOLLOW EACH STEP IDENTICALLY AS I SHOW IN THE VIDEO
the next step in this process is just. Funding your contract
We'll front-run all the retail investors that come in
will automatically sell within a minute

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker's profit claims are forceful, but they are not presented as a fixed payout for every viewer. He describes competing with other bots, calls his own results "really good luck," and says a deposit back usually takes a few minutes. He also acknowledges that some newly launched tokens may be rug pulls. Those qualifications do not verify the bot or make the funding step prudent. They do, however, leave room to read this as a risky trading demonstration rather than a promise that following the steps will produce the same return.

citations.quote: you'll only be competing. With other bots on the mempool
I've had really good luck with this the last few weeks
we usually only need to wait a few minutes before. We get a deposit back into our address
everyone's coming out with their. New little rug pull shit coin

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited earnings claim reports what the speaker says happened to him; it does not, by itself, establish a promised return to each viewer. Funding a contract and pressing its Action button are consequential steps, but those steps alone do not show where the funds ultimately go. His explanation of competing for trades also complicates a reading of the returns as assured. The claims deserve scrutiny, but the opening's lack of verified returns is a limit on what can be concluded from this record, not proof of deception.

citations.quote: I'll show you how I earned 9.4 BNB, that's almost 5.000 U$D, with a front running bot I created by myself.
you'll only be competing. With other bots on the mempool

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Acknowledging competition or describing past results as luck does not undo the video's direct instruction to reproduce the process. The description says the bot works perfectly, tells viewers to follow every step identically, and supplies a contract to paste into Remix. The demonstration then moves from deployment to funding that contract. The defense's qualifiers do not establish that the contract performs the claimed trades or sends profits back; they sit beside an actionable funding instruction and unusually large return claims.

citations.quote: THE BOT WORKS PERFECTLY AND IS UPDATED TO 6/01/2022
PLEASE FOLLOW EACH STEP IDENTICALLY AS I SHOW IN THE VIDEO
4 Paste SmartContract to Remix: https://pastebin.com/raw/x0gj0ksM
the next step in this process is just. Funding your contract

opening.argument: Judge, the video's organizing structure is a software walkthrough. The speaker starts in Remix, creates a contract file, identifies the compiler version, connects a wallet, deploys, and checks for an address on BSCScan. The sampled frames show the editor and deployment interface. That sequence gives viewers something concrete to inspect: how he says this contract is built and operated. His claimed return is a reason to question the demonstration's credibility, but it need not displace its central subject, an operational tutorial about a trading bot.

citations.quote: This. Is where we're going to be building our contract.
Solidity and that's it let me go compile front run bot there we go it compiled.
I copied that, paste it in BSC scan. You can see. That there's an address there now

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution accurately identifies the external contract, funding step, and stated returns. But those details also form the sequence being demonstrated; their presence does not alone prove that the speaker's account of what the contract does is false. A deployed address shows deployment, not profitable trading, while the absence of verified returns limits both the speaker's claim and any definitive conclusion about the outcome. The closer question is whether the video is chiefly explaining a procedure or simply using that procedure to solicit funds.

citations.quote: 4 Paste SmartContract to Remix: https://pastebin.com/raw/x0gj0ksM
You can see. That there's an address there now so the next step in this process is just. Funding your contract

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough format is precisely how the video directs viewers toward the risky step. It does not stop at showing an editor or explaining Solidity: the speaker tells viewers to fund the deployed contract and then press Action, while claiming the bot automatically buys and sells and returns most profits to their wallets. Compilation and a visible address cannot establish those behaviors. Calling the sequence a tutorial does not answer the concern that it promotes funding an unverified contract for purported rapid returns.

citations.quote: we're gonna send. Some funds to that contract that we just created
Here and press the action button the action button then engages all the. Constructors that I built in as far as engaging the pancake router it. Automatically buys and sells for you
90% of the profit is automatically transferred back to your wallet

opening.argument: Judge, this record does not show a request to transfer funds to a named seller or buy access to a service. The speaker describes deploying a contract to the viewer's connected wallet, checking its address, and funding "that contract that we just created." He also says 90% of profits would return to the viewer's wallet. None of that proves the contract is safe: its actual behavior and the claimed returns remain unverified here. But the visible pitch is for operating a trading contract, not an identified fee, credential handover, or payment to the speaker.

citations.quote: So we're going to deploy this to our wallet
I copied that, paste it in BSC scan. You can see. That there's an address there now
we're gonna send. Some funds to that contract that we just created
90% of the profit is automatically transferred back to your wallet

rebuttal.rebuttal: The funding instruction is real, and the return claims are not independently verified by the cited excerpts. Still, the prosecution's quotes do not establish who controls the deployed contract after funding, what its code actually executes, or whether any viewer's funds were lost. Even its quoted mechanism describes purported trades against other market participants, not a payment to the speaker. Those missing facts matter before treating the described trading workflow as a demonstrated diversion of funds.

citations.quote: the next step in this process is just. Funding your contract
We'll front-run all the retail investors that come in

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A request for a named fee or credentials is not necessary to the concern here. The video supplies code from an external link, tells viewers to fund the resulting contract, and claims that pressing Action will generate automated trades and send profits back. Calling it "your contract" does not establish who can move its funds or that the advertised trading logic works. The claimed 15x result amplifies the inducement while remaining unverified by the material cited in the defense.
